Scarcity is the point: the businesses AI trusts are few, and structured data + cross-surface consistency + reviews are what earn that trust.

**2. The mechanism is site-side and concrete.** Google's own developer guidance for agent-friendly sites is specific: actionable elements in semantic HTML, stable layout, interactive elements visibly rendered (>8 sq px, `cursor: pointer`, no ghost overlays) ([localfalcon.com](https://www.localfalcon.com/blog/google-adding-search-agents-expanding-agentic-booking-capabilities-in-local-search)). That is exactly the clean-structure work King Maker bakes in — the site an AI agent can actually read and book on. SEO firms reading Google further argue an agent builds a "Pattern of Consensus" across surfaces and skips a business with conflicting hours or a dead-end static form ([ignitevisibility.com](https://ignitevisibility.com/google-agentic-ai/)) — that risk/consensus model is agency interpretation, not documented Google policy, so we cite Google's actual dev guide for the hard claim and label the rest as how the industry reads it.

### The clock, not the flood

Local intent is structurally insulated today — Google routes "near me" and "[city] + [service]" to the Map Pack and shows AI Overviews on transactional queries only ~5% of the time ([geoaiomarketing.com](https://geoaiomarketing.com/the-types-of-queries-that-never-trigger-ai-overviews/)). But that is a current design choice, not a permanent guarantee (Google tested "near me" AIOs at 100% in 2023 before pulling them). And where AI does appear, it depresses clicks: an independent Pew browsing panel found users clicked a traditional link 8% of the time with an AI summary present vs 15% without — a ~47% relative drop (n=900 adults, 68,879 searches) ([pewresearch.org](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/)). Google disputes Pew's methodology, so the honest move is to pair it with the randomized CMU/ISB field experiment that found a 38% click reduction on triggered queries ([searchenginejournal.com](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/ai-overviews-cut-organic-clicks-38-field-study-finds/573145/)). Net: insulation is a now-advantage with a shelf life — which is the whole reason to build the AI-readable site before it erodes.

**What NOT to oversell: AI is not a lead channel yet (~1-2% of organic) — we sell agent-readability and the scarcity of AI recommendation, never "AI leads convert better" (the underlying study shows the opposite) and never a precise "0.3% / 81,329-lead" figure (no public source).**

loadBearing.claim: Being recommended by AI is 3-30x harder than ranking in traditional local search — AI excludes most businesses entirely, making AI recommendation a scarce, defensible position.
loadBearing.stat: 3-30x harder; ChatGPT recommended 1.2% of locations, Gemini 11%, Perplexity 7.4%, vs 35.9% appearing in Google's local 3-pack
loadBearing.snippet: AI visibility is three to 30 times harder to achieve than ranking well in traditional local search ... 1.2% of locations were recommended by ChatGPT, 11% by Gemini, and 7.4% by Perplexity ... brands appeared in Google's local 3-pack 35.9% of the time. ... AI systems prioritize confidence and risk reduction over breadth.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the core scarcity / future-proofing argument and the cleanest independent source for it. It's the slide that justifies 'build the AI-ready site now' without claiming AI is a volume channel. Verified verbatim at gather time.

loadBearing.claim: AI referral traffic is ~1% of all website visits today and is overwhelmingly ChatGPT — so 'AI as a traffic channel' is not yet real at scale.
loadBearing.stat: ~1% of all website visits from AI; ChatGPT = 87.4% of AI referrals; 13,770 domains / 3.3B sessions
loadBearing.snippet: AI referral traffic accounts for just over 1% of all website visits across 10 major industries ... ChatGPT drove 87.4% of all AI referrals across the dataset ... Conductor analyzed 13,770 domains across 10 GICS-aligned industries, looking at more than 3.3 billion sessions.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the honesty anchor — the number a skeptic will demand. Leading with it (large-N, independent) inoculates the whole pillar and lets us sell future-proofing instead of volume. Verified verbatim at gather time.

loadBearing.claim: When an AI summary appears, users click traditional links far less — independent behavioral (not survey) data shows a ~47% relative drop.
loadBearing.stat: Clicked a traditional link 8% of the time with an AI summary vs 15% without; n=900 US adults, 68,879 searches, March 2025
loadBearing.snippet: Users who encountered an AI summary clicked on a traditional search result link in 8% of all visits. Those who did not encounter an AI summary clicked on a search result nearly twice as often (15% of visits). ... 900 U.S. adults ... 68,879 unique Google searches.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Quantifies the erosion threat that justifies acting now. It's a measured browsing panel, not a survey. MUST be paired with the CMU/ISB RCT because Google formally disputes Pew's methodology — a skeptic will lead with that rebuttal. Verified verbatim at gather time.

loadBearing.claim: Google's own developer guidance for agent-friendly sites is concrete and site-side — semantic HTML, stable layout, visibly-rendered actionable elements — which is exactly the clean-structure work King Maker bakes in.
loadBearing.stat: Semantic HTML + stable layout + visible actionable elements (>8 sq px, cursor:pointer, no ghost overlays)
loadBearing.snippet: Actionable elements should be designed with semantic HTML ... Avoid hiding interactive elements (e.g., with 'ghost' elements or transparent overlays) ... All interactive elements should be visible in an area larger than 8 square pixels ... Signal cursor actionability by setting cursor: pointer.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Ties the abstract future-proofing pitch to a concrete deliverable KM ships. The underlying guidance is Google first-party (relayed via LocalFalcon); cite Google's dev guide as the authority, not the agency framing. Quoted via secondary source — confirm against Google's primary dev doc before it goes on a slide.

loadBearing.claim: Local/transactional contractor queries are structurally insulated from AI Overviews today — but it's a current Google design choice with a shelf life, not a permanent guarantee.
loadBearing.stat: AIOs trigger on ~5% of transactional queries; 'near me' AIO ~0% (routed to Map Pack); Google tested near-me AIOs at 100% in 2023 before pulling them
loadBearing.snippet: local intent queries with 'near me' or '[city] + [service]' trigger the Local Pack instead of an AI Overview ... transactional queries show AIOs 5% of the time.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Supports the 'now-advantage with a clock' frame that makes the future-proofing pitch urgent rather than hypothetical. Vendor source with a selling incentive; corroborated directionally by the Semrush 10M-keyword study (transactional ~14% AIO). Frame as insulation that erodes, never as 'local will never be disrupted.'

whatNotToOversell: AI is NOT a lead-volume channel yet — keep the number honest at ~1-2% of organic leads / ~1% of traffic. Anyone pitching AI traffic as a 2026 faucet gets pulled apart by a skeptic.

Do NOT claim 'AI leads convert better' or 'AI leads are ~2x quality.' The underlying SearchLight study shows the opposite — AI leads underperformed organic on close rate (29% vs 40%) and booking rate. The bullish version lives only in vendor blogs.
Do NOT put a precise '0.3% / 0.29%' or the '81,329-lead McChesney study' on any slide or reel — no public primary source exists. Use the double-sourced 'low single-digit %' range instead.

Do NOT present the 'Pattern of Consensus / static form = risk / specific star thresholds' as Google policy — that's agency interpretation. Cite Google's actual agent-friendly dev guidance (semantic HTML, stable layout) for hard claims; label the risk-scoring model as how SEO firms read it.
Do NOT hang the click-erosion claim on Pew alone — Google formally disputes its methodology. Always pair it with the randomized CMU/ISB field experiment (38% drop) so the claim survives the rebuttal.

Do NOT promise local search will 'never' be AI-disrupted. Insulation on 'near me' queries is a current Google design choice that has been toggled before; frame it as a now-advantage with a shelf life.
gaps: No public primary source found for the seed's '81,329-lead McChesney study' or the precise 0.29-0.3% AI-lead-share figure — could not double-confirm; treated as directional/unverified.

No Google FIRST-PARTY document found stating an explicit reviews/ratings threshold (e.g., 4.5★+) or 'static contact form = risk' for agentic booking — those specifics are agency interpretation. Google's primary doc covers agent-friendly site mechanics, not selection thresholds.

The SearchLight/Torrey volume data (1.74%, 83% ChatGPT) is single-agency-origin; corroborated for the general 'AI is ~1% of traffic' magnitude by independent Conductor/SEL data, but not the exact contractor-lead percentage.

Lead-quality direction is genuinely contested: the primary study shows AI leads UNDERperform on close rate, while secondary blogs claim higher conversion. No independent dataset resolves which is true for contractors specifically.

Agentic booking for HOME SERVICES specifically is still on Google's roadmap (currently restaurants/tickets/wellness in Search Labs) — home-services rollout timing is hinted, not confirmed, so 'summer 2026' for contractors is directional.

Did not independently re-verify the SOCi 1.2%/11%/7.4% recommendation rates against SOCi's own published index PDF (relied on SEL's independent reporting of it) — SEL is a strong independent secondary, but the raw index was not opened.

No NC/Triangle/Raleigh-specific or roofing-vertical-specific AI-search lead or citation data was found in any independent primary source. All vertical-specific numbers (e.g. SearchLight's contractor study from round 1) remain single-origin; roofing-specific claims should stay national + directional.

The ~0.3%/0.29% 'share of contractor leads from AI' figure remains UNVERIFIED in any public primary source after a second pass — treat as directional only. The defensible double-sourced figure is still 'low single-digit % of leads/traffic' (round-1 SearchLight 1.74% + Conductor ~1%).

The agentic-booking grounding requirements (Pattern of Consensus, ReserveAction/LocalBusiness/Service schema, 'static form = risk') still trace primarily to agency analyses (Ignite Visibility, Local Falcon) interpreting Google docs, plus Google's own developer agent-guidance. A direct Google first-party statement that a 'static contact form' gets a business SKIPPED for a competitor was not located — that specific causal claim should be attributed to the agency interpretation, not to Google.

Schema-to-AI-citation multipliers (45% LocalBusiness, 2.8x FAQ) are single-source vendor correlations with no independent causal corroborator found — keep as directional, do not present as measured causation.

Largely SATURATED on the core thesis: across diverse searches the same cluster of sources (Pew, Agarwal/Sen RCT, Semrush 10M, BrightLocal LCRS, SOCi/SEL) recurs. Net-new beyond round 1 is mainly STRONGER sourcing (academic RCT, Pew primary, BrightLocal primary, Semrush intent-breakdown) and the reconciled trigger-rate nuance + Google's formal rebuttal — not new claim categories.

counter.point: The 'AI leads are ~2x quality' seed claim is CONTRADICTED by the underlying study's own data. Jon Torrey/SearchLight reports AI-referred leads UNDERperform: just 29% of the LLM revenue pipeline closed vs a 40% paid+organic average, and AI booking rates (31-35%) trailed organic's 43.2%. The favorable '73% conversion vs 31%' / '2x quality' numbers circulate in vendor BLOGS, not in the primary study — do not sell 'AI leads close better' as fact.
counter.soWhat: Sell future-proofing + agent-readability + scarcity of AI recommendation — NOT 'AI leads convert higher.' The quality claim is contested and the bullish version is unsourced/vendor-amplified; leading with it invites a skeptic to pull the same study and find the opposite.

counter.point: AI lead ATTRIBUTION is badly broken — in the same study only 1.5% of AI leads were correctly attributed in CRMs (69.8% no attribution, 28.7% misattributed). So even the 'AI leads' counts are noisy and likely understated/messy on both directions.
counter.soWhat: Be honest that nobody can cleanly measure AI lead share yet; this cuts BOTH ways (real volume may be higher than tracked, but so is the uncertainty). Frame as 'measurement is immature,' reinforcing 'don't bank on it as a 2026 volume channel.'

counter.point: The 0.3%/0.29% and the '81,329-lead McChesney study' have no locatable public primary source. The double-confirmation claimed in the seed could not be reproduced from open web sources.
counter.soWhat: Do not put a precise 0.3% on a deck or reel slide as a sourced stat. Use 'low single-digit % of leads (≈1-2% of organic, ~1% of traffic)' which IS double-sourced (Torrey + Conductor/SEL).

counter.point: Most agentic-booking grounding specifics (Pattern of Consensus, 'static form = risk') come from AGENCY blogs interpreting Google, not Google's own words. Google's first-party guidance is the agent-friendly-website dev guide (semantic HTML, stable layout) — solid — but the reviews/ratings thresholds and 'risk' scoring are agency inference, not documented Google policy.
counter.soWhat: Cite Google's actual dev guidance for the hard claims; label the consensus/risk model as 'how SEO firms read it,' not Google policy. Avoids overclaiming a specific 4.5★ threshold Google never published.

counter.point: AI Overview suppression on local intent is a current Google design choice, not a permanent guarantee — Google tested 'near me' AIOs at 100% in 2023 before pulling them. The KM prior already assumes insulation erodes on a ~12-month clock.
counter.soWhat: Frame insulation as a NOW-advantage with a shelf life — which actually strengthens the future-proofing pitch (build the AI-readable site before the insulation erodes), but don't promise local search will 'never' be AI-disrupted.

counter.point: Google formally disputes the Pew study as methodologically flawed: 'This study uses a flawed methodology and skewed queryset that is not representative of Search traffic,' and says it has 'not observed significant drops in aggregate web traffic.' Google's John Mueller argues remaining post-AIO clicks are higher-quality (users 'spend more time on the site'). A skeptic will lead with this — so the defensible KM position is to cite the independent academic RCT (Agarwal/Sen) and Pew TOGETHER, not Pew alone.
counter.soWhat: Don't hang the click-erosion claim on any single study. The randomized CMU/ISB experiment is the strongest rebuttal to Google's 'unrepresentative queryset' objection because it RANDOMIZED users rather than cherry-picking queries — lead with it.

counter.point: The 'local intent is insulated' thesis has a real counter: some 2026 vendor data claims AIOs now appear in 68% of local searches overall (Whitespark Q2 2026), with 92% of informational-local and 97% of hybrid/pricing local queries triggering AIOs. A skeptic will wave the 68% headline.
counter.soWhat: Reconcilable but you must state the nuance honestly: '68% of local searches' bundles informational/hybrid local queries (which DO trigger AIOs heavily) with pure transactional 'plumber near me' (which the Semrush 10M study shows trigger AIOs only ~14%, routed to the Map Pack instead). The insulation is specific to high-intent transactional/navigational queries, NOT all 'local' queries. Claiming broad local immunity is overclaiming.

counter.point: The same RCT that measures a 38% click cut also found removing AI Overviews 'didn't change reported satisfaction, perceived quality, or ease of finding information.' A skeptic can argue AIOs aren't degrading the user's journey — meaning the homeowner may still reach a contractor, just via a different path.
counter.soWhat: Reinforces that the threat is to TRAFFIC ROUTING (who gets cited/clicked), not to demand. KM's pitch should be 'be the business AI routes to,' not 'AI is destroying contractor demand' — the latter is false and a skeptic will puncture it.

counter.point: Adoption stats are survey self-report of USAGE/INTENT (BrightLocal 45% 'have used AI to find a local business'), not measured LEAD VOLUME. Round 1 already established AI is ~1-2% of actual organic lead/traffic volume. The gap between '45% have tried AI' and '~1-2% of leads come from AI' is large and a skeptic will exploit it.
counter.soWhat: Keep the two numbers in separate buckets and never conflate them: adoption/curiosity is high and rising fast; realized lead VOLUME is still low-single-digit %. The honest frame is a leading-indicator/erosion-clock story, not a 'leads are flooding in from AI' story.

counter.point: Semrush's own data shows AIO prevalence is not a one-way ramp: zero-click rate on tracked keywords actually DECREASED slightly (33.75% -> 31.53%) before/after AIO appeared on the same keywords, and a separate SEL analysis noted AIOs 'surged in 2025, then pulled back.' The cannibalization narrative is noisier than the doomsday version.
counter.soWhat: Avoid apocalyptic framing. The defensible claim is 'directional erosion of the insulation over ~12 months,' explicitly labeled directional — not a precise or monotonic collapse.

allClaims.claim: AI/LLM referrals are a rounding error on lead and traffic VOLUME today for local/home-services — roughly 1-2% of organic, not a flood. The SearchLight Q1 2026 study of 707 contractors found LLMs generated 1.74% of organic's lead volume.
allClaims.stat: 1.74% of organic lead volume (2,337 AI leads across 707 contractors, Q1 2026)
allClaims.snippet: LLMs Generated 1.74% of Organic's Lead Volume in Q1 ... 2,337 AI-referred leads ... 707 home services contractors.

allClaims.claim: Independent cross-industry data corroborates that AI referral is ~1% of all website traffic and ChatGPT dominates it — so 'AI as a volume channel' is not yet real at scale. Conductor analyzed 13,770 domains / 3.3B sessions (May-Sep 2025).
allClaims.stat: ~1% of all website visits from AI; ChatGPT = 87.4% of AI referrals
allClaims.snippet: AI referral traffic accounts for just over 1% of all website visits across 10 major industries ... ChatGPT drove 87.4% of all AI referrals across the dataset ... 13,770 domains ... more than 3.3 billion sessions.

allClaims.claim: The precise ~0.3% / 0.29% 'share of contractor leads from AI' figure (and the '81,329-lead McChesney study') could NOT be located in any public primary source. It is single-origin and should be treated as DIRECTIONAL only; the defensible, double-sourced framing is 'low single-digit % of leads/traffic.'
allClaims.stat: 0.29-0.3% — UNVERIFIED public source (closest public anchors: 1.74% of organic leads, ~1% of traffic)
allClaims.snippet: LLMs Generated 1.74% of Organic's Lead Volume in Q1 — the public SearchLight number; no public page surfaces an 81,329-lead study or a 0.29% figure under the name McChesney.

allClaims.claim: Local/transactional intent is structurally INSULATED from AI Overviews — Google removed AIOs from 'near me' queries and routes local intent to the Map Pack, so the bread-and-butter contractor query is not (yet) cannibalized by AI. BrightLocal 2026 found just 4-8% AIO/local-pack overlap.
allClaims.stat: ~5% AIO trigger on transactional queries; 4-8% local-pack/AIO overlap; 'near me' AIO ~0%
allClaims.snippet: local intent queries with 'near me' or '[city] + [service]' trigger the Local Pack instead of an AI Overview ... transactional queries show AIOs 5% of the time.

allClaims.claim: Google's agentic booking (rolling out in AI Mode, 2026) GROUNDS its recommendation on the business's structured data and cross-surface consistency: it builds a 'Pattern of Consensus' by crawling multiple surfaces, and a business with inconsistent hours/services or a 'static contact form' is flagged a 'risk' and skipped for a competitor.
allClaims.stat: Qualitative grounding model — consensus across GBP/Yelp/Apple/Facebook/website; static contact form = risk → skipped
allClaims.snippet: the system develops a 'Pattern of Consensus' by crawling multiple digital surfaces ... if AI identifies conflicting data like inconsistently listed hours or services, or detects a technical dead-end like a static contact form, the business is considered a 'risk' and the AI agent moves to a competing business.

allClaims.claim: Google's own developer guidance for agent-friendly websites is concrete and site-side: actionable elements must be in semantic HTML, layout must be stable, interactive elements must be visibly rendered (no ghost/transparent overlays, >8 sq px, cursor:pointer). This is exactly the structured/clean-site work King Maker bakes in — 'the site the AI can actually book on.'
allClaims.stat: Semantic HTML + stable layout + visible actionable elements (>8 sq px) — Google agent-friendly guide
allClaims.snippet: All necessary actions (i.e., that a human or agent could take) should be clearly reflected in the site's interface ... Actionable elements should be designed with semantic HTML ... Avoid hiding interactive elements (e.g., with 'ghost' elements or transparent overlays) ... All interactive elements should be visible in an area larger than 8 square pixels ... Signal cursor actionability by setting cursor: pointer.

allClaims.claim: Being RECOMMENDED by AI is 3-30x harder than ranking in traditional local search — AI excludes most businesses entirely. SOCi's 2026 Local Visibility Index: ChatGPT recommended only 1.2% of locations, Gemini 11%, Perplexity 7.4%, vs 35.9% appearing in Google's local 3-pack. This is the 'scarcity = future-proofing premium' case, from an independent SEL report.
allClaims.stat: 3-30x harder; ChatGPT 1.2%, Gemini 11%, Perplexity 7.4% of locations recommended vs 35.9% local 3-pack
allClaims.snippet: AI visibility is three to 30 times harder to achieve than ranking well in traditional local search ... 1.2% of locations were recommended by ChatGPT, 11% by Gemini, and 7.4% by Perplexity ... brands appeared in Google's local 3-pack 35.9% of the time.

allClaims.claim: AI selects on CONFIDENCE, not ranking — middling-rated businesses that still rank by proximity get excluded entirely from AI results. This is why structured data, accurate cross-surface info, and reviews/reputation (not just ranking) are the future-proofing levers.
allClaims.stat: Qualitative — AI prioritizes 'confidence and risk reduction over breadth'
allClaims.snippet: In AI-driven results, SOCi found those same locations are frequently excluded altogether, as AI systems prioritize confidence and risk reduction over breadth.

allClaims.claim: Citation rates differ ~46x by engine — so 'getting cited by AI' is engine-specific and hard, not a uniform faucet. A 2026 study of 34,234 AI responses: ChatGPT cited brands 0.59% of the time, Perplexity 13.05%, Grok 27%. ChatGPT answers mostly from parametric memory, not live citations.
allClaims.stat: ChatGPT 0.59% vs Perplexity 13.05% vs Grok 27% citation rate (34,234 responses)
allClaims.snippet: A separate 2026 study of 34,234 AI responses found a 46-times difference in brand citation rates between platforms — ChatGPT cited brands just 0.59% of the time while Perplexity sat at 13.05%. Grok came in even higher at 27%.

allClaims.claim: Recommended structured-data for agentic local booking is explicit: LocalBusiness, Service, and ReserveAction schema make a business 'understandable to AI systems' — concrete schema King Maker can ship as a future-proofing deliverable.
allClaims.stat: LocalBusiness + Service + ReserveAction schema; 'Reserve with Google' integration
allClaims.snippet: Implementation of schema markup (LocalBusiness, Service, ReserveAction) makes business information 'understandable to AI systems' ... Integration with Google-partnered scheduling software enables actual reservations through 'Reserve with Google' functionality.

allClaims.claim: ChatGPT is the overwhelmingly dominant AI lead source among the engines — so 'AI search' for contractors today effectively means ChatGPT. SearchLight Q1 2026: ChatGPT = 83% of all AI leads, 10x Gemini's volume.
allClaims.stat: ChatGPT 83% of AI leads, 10x Gemini
allClaims.snippet: ChatGPT generated 83% of all AI leads and generated 10x the volume of Google Gemini.

allClaims.claim: Homeowner adoption of AI to FIND contractors is rising fast even though the lead share is still tiny — supporting the 'build for the clock, not for today' future-proofing frame (KM ~12-month insulation-erosion thesis). Reported ~22-45% of homeowners now use AI tools in the contractor search.
allClaims.stat: ~22-45% of homeowners use AI tools to research/find contractors (directional, secondary)
allClaims.snippet: 22% of homeowners now use AI tools like ChatGPT to research and find contractors ... 45% of homeowners are using AI tools to find contractors.

allClaims.claim: Independent academic RCT (the highest-quality source on this question) measures AI Overviews cutting organic clicks ~38% on triggered queries, with zero-click rising from 54% to 72% — but the SAME experiment found removing AIOs did not change user satisfaction, a nuance that matters for honest framing.
allClaims.stat: AI Overviews reduced organic clicks on triggered queries by 38%; zero-click rose 54%->72%; AIOs appeared on 42% of queries; effect strongest when AIO at top (85% of occurrences); n=1,065 randomized US desktop Chrome users, Jan-Feb 2026.
allClaims.snippet: AI Overviews reduced organic clicks on triggered queries by 38% ... zero-click searches rising from 54% to 72%. The working paper was conducted by Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen from the Indian School of Business and Carnegie Mellon University. A Chrome extension randomly assigned 1,065 U.S. desktop Chrome users to three groups over two weeks (January-February 2026). ... Removing AI Overviews didn't change reported satisfaction, perceived quality, or ease of finding information.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (pre-registered randomized controlled experiment, AEA RCT Registry; draft on SSRN, awaiting peer review)

allClaims.claim: Pew Research (independent primary, browsing-data panel) is the strongest single corroborator that AIOs depress clicks: users clicked a traditional link 8% of the time when an AI summary appeared vs 15% without (a ~47% relative drop), and ended their session more often. This is a behavioral, not survey, measurement.
allClaims.stat: Clicked a traditional link: 8% with AI summary vs 15% without (~47% relative reduction); clicked a link inside the summary only 1%; ended session 26% (AIO) vs 16% (no AIO). n=900 US adults, 68,879 searches, 12,593 with AI summaries, March 1-31 2025.
allClaims.snippet: Users who encountered an AI summary clicked on a traditional search result link in 8% of all visits. Those who did not encounter an AI summary clicked on a search result nearly twice as often (15% of visits). ... Sample size: 900 U.S. adults. Study period: March 1-31, 2025. Total searches analyzed: 68,879.

allClaims.claim: Semrush's 10M+ keyword study (large-N, independent of the local-SEO vendors) gives the strongest evidence for the structural-insulation thesis: transactional queries trigger AIOs only ~14% and navigational ~10%, vs ~57% for informational. The contractor's bread-and-butter lower-funnel query is far less AIO-exposed than informational content.
allClaims.stat: As of Nov 2025: informational 57.1% AIO trigger, commercial 18.57%, transactional 13.94%, navigational 10.33% (lowest). Down from 91.3% of AIO-triggering queries being informational in Jan 2025.
allClaims.snippet: informational queries show AI Overviews at 57.1%, compared to commercial at 18.57%, transactional at 13.94%, and navigational at 10.33%.

allClaims.claim: HONEST EROSION SIGNAL (supports KM's 'build for the clock, not for today' frame without overclaiming): the same Semrush dataset shows AIOs migrating DOWN-funnel fast — navigational-query AIO triggering went from 0.74% (Jan 2025) to 10.33% (Oct 2025). The insulation of transactional/local intent is real today but visibly shrinking, which is the defensible version of the future-proofing case.
allClaims.stat: Navigational-query AIO trigger rate rose from 0.74% (January 2025) to 10.33% (October 2025) — a >13x increase in ~9 months; AIOs 'starting to target lower-funnel searches.'
allClaims.snippet: navigational searches that trigger AI Overviews have skyrocketed from 0.74% in January to 10.33% in October. ... AI Overviews are slowly but surely starting to target lower-funnel searches.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured trend (directional extrapolation to future erosion)

allClaims.claim: BrightLocal's LCRS 2026 (independent primary, n=1,002 US consumers) is a stronger corroborator than round-1's adoption sources: 45% of consumers now use AI to find local businesses, up from 6% a year prior — AI is the 3rd most-used local-discovery channel behind Google and Facebook. This grounds the 'adoption is rising fast even while lead share is tiny' future-proofing frame.
allClaims.stat: 45% of consumers use AI tools for local business recommendations (up from 6% in 2025, ~7.5x); 3rd most-used discovery channel behind Google and Facebook; highest adoption age 30-44 at 64%; ChatGPT leads at 31% of AI users.
allClaims.snippet: the proportion of consumers using AI to find local business recommendations has climbed from 6% in 2025 to 45% today ... AI is now the third most-used tool for local recommendations, behind Google and Facebook. ... Survey size: 1,002 US adult consumers via SurveyMonkey.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (survey self-report; intent/usage not actual lead volume)

allClaims.claim: BrightLocal also quantifies the TRUST gap that makes AI a discovery channel, not yet a closing channel: 42% trust AI equally with online reviews, but 88-97% of AI users still double-check AI suggestions against native review platforms. Useful honest framing — AI is becoming a top-of-funnel referrer for contractors, not a replacement for reviews/reputation.
allClaims.stat: 42% of consumers trust AI tools equally with online reviews; among active AI users 63% trust AI recommendations; 88% verify recommendations / 97% sometimes double-check against review platforms.
allClaims.snippet: 42% of consumers trust AI tools equally with online reviews ... 88% of AI users verify recommendations by checking legitimacy or sources ... 97% sometimes double-check AI suggestions against native review platforms.

allClaims.claim: SOCi's 1.2% AI-recommendation figure (round-1 SEL source) traces to a 350,000+ location analysis — a larger, more concrete base than the original framing implied, strengthening the 'scarcity = future-proofing premium' case (most businesses get recommended by AI essentially never).
allClaims.stat: Only 1.2% of local business locations ever get recommended by AI search (SOCi, 350,000+ locations analyzed).
allClaims.source_type: agency-blog (citing SOCi; corroborates round-1 SEL report)
allClaims.snippet: only 1.2 percent of local business locations ever get recommended by AI search (SOCi, 350,000+ locations analyzed).
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (vendor index; corroborates the independent SEL 2026 Local Visibility report already in round 1)

allClaims.claim: Structured-data is a measurable AI-citation lever, not just theory — quantified figures exist for the schema work KM bakes in. Treat the exact multipliers as DIRECTIONAL (vendor-sourced) but the direction is well-supported across sources.
allClaims.stat: LocalBusiness schema associated with ~45% higher AI citation rate (Semrush); pages with FAQ schema ~2.8x more likely to be cited in AI answers (FogLift 2026).
allClaims.snippet: Properly implemented LocalBusiness schema = 45 percent higher AI citation rate (Semrush) ... Pages with FAQ schema are 2.8x more likely to be cited in AI answers (FogLift 2026).
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: directional (vendor correlation, not causal; single-source per stat)

pillars.title: Platform-tier / scaling headroom
pillars.section:
## P9 — Platform-tier / scaling headroom

**Bottom line: the cheap template/builder tier is the right place to *start* and the wrong place to *scale*. The ceiling is not aesthetic — it is data ownership, page-scale, performance, and Google spam-policy exposure, and it bites specifically as a contractor adds crews, markets, and content. It does not bite on day one, and a customized build can scale fine.** This is a headroom argument, not a "templates can't work" argument.

**1. The largest, highest-traffic sites diversify off the default CMS as they scale.** WordPress powers ~59.3% of all CMS-detected sites overall, but only 46.8% of the top-1,000 highest-traffic sites ([w3techs.com](https://w3techs.com/technologies/cross/content_management/ranking)). That is a *drop*, not a collapse — nearly half of even the biggest sites still run WordPress. The honest read: the default tier scales until differentiation, performance, and ownership start to matter, then operators move.

**2. Google's spam policy names the exact failure mode of template-sprawl.** "Doorway abuse" (pages built to rank for similar queries that don't help users) and "scaled content abuse" (many pages generated mainly to manipulate rankings) are both enumerated, enforceable violations ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)). Near-identical city/location pages — the template tier's default way to "cover more markets" — are squarely in scope. Note the trigger is *thin, near-identical value*, not a shared layout: Google dedupes duplicate content, it does not auto-penalize a shared theme. The risk is reduced visibility plus spam-policy exposure for thin pages, which a multi-market contractor hits as page count grows.

**3. The all-in-one builder tier has no supported exit.** GoHighLevel — the canonical local lead-gen template stack — states in its own support docs: "HighLevel does not support exporting websites in a way that allows them to be managed or edited outside the HighLevel platform... There is no supported 1:1 website export" ([help.gohighlevel.com](https://help.gohighlevel.com/support/solutions/articles/155000007342-can-highlevel-websites-be-exported-)). Rendered HTML can be copied manually, so this is a real switching cost — lossy, unsupported migration — not literal impossibility. The demand is documented: contractors upvote an open request to export GHL sites to WordPress on GHL's own ideas board ([ideas.gohighlevel.com](https://ideas.gohighlevel.com/website/p/be-able-to-export-the-website-created-in-ghl-outside-ghl-to-clients-current-host)).

**4. The default tier carries a measured performance ceiling — without ongoing expert tuning.** Field data (HTTP Archive / Google CrUX) shows WordPress origins pass Core Web Vitals at ~40% (2024, up from 28% in 2023), below the 51% all-origin global average, while purpose-built managed platforms outperform it: Duda 73%, TYPO3 71%, Squarespace 60% ([almanac.httparchive.org](https://almanac.httparchive.org/en/2024/cms)). Two honest caveats: WordPress is improving fast, and properly-tuned WordPress can match a managed platform's baseline. The ceiling is about the *unmanaged default state* — which is precisely the value of a build engineered for consistent performance without per-site configuration. Why it matters for contractors: Google's own research found mobile bounce probability rises 123% as load goes 1s→10s ([business.google.com](https://business.google.com/ca-en/think/marketing-strategies/mobile-page-speed-new-industry-benchmarks/)) — slowness directly costs mobile-heavy contractor traffic.

**5. Scaled operators run a split stack the all-in-one tier collapses.** Established multi-crew home-service businesses typically pair a marketing CMS with a dedicated field-service ops platform; ServiceTitan-class tools concede they fit "established mid- to large-sized" businesses and are "not a great option for sole proprietors or small businesses" ([servicetitan.com](https://www.servicetitan.com/blog/home-services-websites)) — vendor-incentive source, directional. The all-in-one builder folds website and ops into one tool, which becomes the integration ceiling as the operation grows.

**What NOT to oversell:** never say "templates/WordPress can't scale" — false, and a skeptic kills it instantly (many 7-figure roofers run customized WordPress). Never say "duplicate templates get you penalized" — the trigger is thin unique value, not shared layout. Never say "you can never get your site out of GHL" — say "no supported migration path." Never imply the default CMS is permanently slow — it is the *unmanaged* state that lags, and that gap is what a managed build closes.

loadBearing.claim: WordPress's share of CMS-built sites drops from 59.3% overall to 46.8% among the top-1,000 highest-traffic sites — the largest web properties diversify off the dominant default-template CMS as they scale.
loadBearing.stat: WordPress: 59.3% overall vs 50.9% (top 10k) vs 46.8% (top 1k) of CMS-detected sites
loadBearing.snippet: WordPress percentages by ranking: Overall 59.3%; Top 100,000 51.6%; Top 10,000 50.9%; Top 1,000 46.8%.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the headline 'biggest sites outgrow the default tier' proof point for a slide/reel; independent measurement, verified verbatim at gather time.

loadBearing.claim: Google's spam policy names doorway abuse and scaled content abuse as enforceable violations — the exact failure mode of duplicated multi-market city pages from the template tier.
loadBearing.stat: Two named, enforceable spam categories: doorway abuse + scaled content abuse
loadBearing.snippet: Doorway abuse: sites or pages created to rank for specific, similar search queries that lead users to intermediate pages not as useful as the final destination. Scaled content abuse: many pages generated for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings and not helping users. Both are enforceable; violating sites 'may rank lower in results or not appear at all.'
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Primary Google source ties the content-ceiling argument to enforceable policy, not opinion — FTC/skeptic-proof. Must be framed as 'thin pages risk enforcement,' not 'shared templates get penalized.'

loadBearing.claim: GoHighLevel — the canonical all-in-one local lead-gen builder — has no supported website export; sites cannot be cleanly migrated to a real CMS, a concrete ownership/switching-cost ceiling.
loadBearing.stat: Zero supported 1:1 export path (per GHL's own support portal)
loadBearing.snippet: HighLevel does not support exporting websites in a way that allows them to be managed or edited outside the HighLevel platform... There is no supported 1:1 website export.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Primary vendor admission of lock-in — the strongest 'you don't own it' proof for a deck. Verified verbatim. Must say 'no supported migration,' not 'impossible,' since rendered HTML is copyable.

loadBearing.claim: Field data shows the default CMS tier (WordPress) passes Core Web Vitals on only ~40% of origins, below the 51% global average, while purpose-built managed platforms outperform it (Duda 73%, TYPO3 71%, Squarespace 60%).
loadBearing.stat: WordPress good-CWV pass rate 40% (2024, up from 28% in 2023) vs 51% global average; Duda 73%, TYPO3 71%, Squarespace 60%
loadBearing.snippet: WordPress had a 28% pass rate in 2023 and 40% in 2024; the global CWV pass rate for all origins as of June 2024 is 51%; Duda (73%), TYPO3 CMS (71%), and Squarespace (60%) outperform WordPress's 40%.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Independent CrUX field-data proof of the performance ceiling — methodologically rigorous, hard for a skeptic to dismiss. Must caveat: it's the UNMANAGED default state; tuned WordPress can close the gap.
loadBearing.measured_or_modeled: measured (CrUX field data, all origins per CMS)

loadBearing.claim: Google's own research found mobile bounce probability rises 123% as page load time goes from 1s to 10s — slowness directly costs the mobile-heavy traffic contractors depend on.
loadBearing.stat: +123% bounce probability as load time goes 1s → 10s (Google / Think with Google)
loadBearing.snippet: as page load time goes from one second to 10 seconds, the probability of a mobile site visitor bouncing increases 123%
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Connects the performance ceiling to lead/revenue impact in a single Google-sourced stat — the 'so what' line for the reel. Verified verbatim. Frame as direction over a load-time range, not a per-second promise.

whatNotToOversell: Do NOT say 'templates/WordPress can't scale' — false and a skeptic kills it instantly; ~47% of even top-1,000 sites still run WordPress, and many 7-figure roofers run customized WordPress fine. The claim is a CHEAP DEFAULT/locked-builder ceiling, not a WordPress ceiling.

Do NOT say 'duplicate templates get you penalized' — Google dedupes duplicate content, it does not auto-penalize shared layout. The enforceable trigger is THIN, near-identical unique value (doorway/scaled-content), not a shared theme.

Do NOT say 'you can never get your site out of GHL' — rendered HTML is copyable and third-party export tools exist. Accurate framing: no vendor-supported 1:1 export, migration is lossy/manual — a real switching cost, not literal impossibility.

Do NOT imply the default CMS is permanently or inherently slow — WordPress went 28%→40% CWV pass in one year and tuned WordPress can match managed-platform baselines. The honest claim is the UNMANAGED default state lags; consistent performance without per-site configuration is the value a managed build adds.

Do NOT claim the platform caps the business or determines rank by itself — local ranking leans heavily on off-page (GBP, reviews, proximity), which a template can support. The defensible thesis is scaling HEADROOM (page-scale, integrations, custom CRO, performance, data ownership), which surfaces as you scale markets — not on day one.

Do NOT present the GHL PageSpeed 20–45 / 'max 60–70' numbers as independently audited — that source is vendor-incentive and self-reported; cite the CrUX field data and GHL's own export admission as the hard corroboration instead.

Do NOT assert specific named roofing brands run on Webflow/headless enterprise stacks — that was not verified. Frame Webflow Enterprise only as a platform CAPABILITY/pattern (AWS+Fastly, headless APIs, large CMS collections), not a brand claim.
gaps: No BuiltWith-style aggregate dataset directly quantifying CMS/platform distribution among SCALED multi-office roofing companies specifically — the W3Techs traffic-tier data is a proxy (all sectors), not roofing-segmented. A roofing-specific BuiltWith tech-stack pull would harden the 'what the scaled tier runs' claim.

Did not verify specific named roofing/home-service brands' stacks (deliberately, to avoid unverified brand claims). The Webflow/headless and WordPress+ServiceTitan patterns are capability/positioning evidence, not a measured census of scaled roofers.

The 32% (1s→3s) bounce stat is widely cited to Google but I could not pin the exact original Think-with-Google page hosting that precise figure; the cleanly-verified primary Google number is 123% for 1s→10s. Treat 32% as directional.

No independent quantification of how often scaling roofers actually MIGRATE off GHL/templates (churn rate / re-platform rate) — the lock-in is documented as a real switching cost but its frequency of biting is anecdotal.

No independent (non-vendor) audit of GoHighLevel PageSpeed/LCP was found — the strongest GHL performance numbers (20–45 mobile, LCP 4–8s, 60–70 cap) trace to a vendor that sells GHL speed fixes (pandacodegen). The DIRECTION is corroborated by GHL's own support docs (toggles only, no SSR control) and by general CSR-vs-SSR research, but the specific numbers want an independent Lighthouse run on real GHL roofing sites. Recommend capturing live PageSpeed scores on 3–5 actual GHL contractor sites as first-party evidence.

No NC/Triangle-specific or named-roofing-brand platform-stack data was verified. Round-1 note holds: frame the scaled stack (WordPress/Webflow marketing layer + ServiceTitan/AccuLynx/JobNimbus ops layer) as a PATTERN, not a brand claim. A first-party survey of what the top ~10 ranking Triangle roofers actually run (BuiltWith/Wappalyzer lookup) would convert this from directional to measured.

The Webflow 58% CWV figure comes from a Webflow-adjacent comparison source; the Web Almanac CMS chapter is the cleaner independent corroborator but its public summary leads with WordPress/Squarespace/Wix/Duda/TYPO3 numbers rather than an explicit Webflow line — worth pulling the exact Webflow figure from the Almanac dataset directly if Webflow is named in the deck.

The AI-crawler-CSR-blindness claim is 2026-current and strategically strong but magnitude varies by crawler and is evolving fast (Google renders JS; OpenAI/Perplexity largely do not) — treat as directional and date-stamp it; it could shift within months.

counter.point: WordPress's share at top-1,000 (46.8%) is a DROP, not a collapse — nearly half of even the highest-traffic CMS sites still run WordPress. WordPress scales fine for huge sites (it powers many enterprise properties). So the honest argument is 'a CHEAP DEFAULT template ceiling,' not 'WordPress/templates can't scale.'
counter.soWhat: Frame the claim precisely as the $297 lead-gen template tier (locked builder + duplicated city pages + bundled performance), NOT as 'templates/WordPress can't grow.' Many 7-figure roofers run perfectly well on a customized WordPress build.

counter.point: Plenty of successful multi-crew roofers DO run on templated/builder stacks and win locally — local ranking leans heavily on GBP, reviews, and proximity (off-page), which a template can support. The site platform is not the sole rank determinant.
counter.soWhat: Don't overclaim that the platform caps the business. The defensible line is scaling HEADROOM: page-scale, integrations, custom UX/CRO, performance, and data ownership — the ceiling appears as you scale markets and need differentiation, not on day one.

counter.point: GHL's rendered HTML CAN be copied/hosted elsewhere, and third-party export tools exist — so 'you can NEVER get your site out' is too strong; it's 'no SUPPORTED, clean migration path.'
counter.soWhat: State the lock-in accurately: no vendor-supported 1:1 export, migration is lossy/manual — a real switching cost, not literal impossibility.

counter.point: Google does NOT penalize duplicate content per se — it filters/dedupes. The risk from templated city pages is reduced visibility + spam-policy exposure for thin doorway pages, not an automatic penalty for shared layout.
counter.soWhat: Use 'thin/near-identical location pages risk doorway/scaled-content enforcement,' not 'duplicate templates get you penalized.' The trigger is thin unique value, not a shared theme.

counter.point: For a SMALL roofing business, a template is the rational, higher-ROI choice — not a defect. Quality templates ship in under a week for $100–300 with built-in SEO, mobile responsiveness, and proven converting layouts, versus 10–14 weeks and $5,000–20,000 for custom. 'Every week without a professional website means losing customers.'
counter.soWhat: Do NOT argue templates can't work or convert — that is false and a skeptic will destroy it. The defensible thesis is narrow: the template/builder tier is the right ENTRY point with a CEILING that bites specifically when a contractor scales (multi-crew, multi-market, content-at-scale, AI-discovery, sub-2.5s mobile). Frame as headroom/outgrowing, never as 'templates are bad.'

counter.point: WordPress itself is improving fast (28% → 40% CWV pass in one year) and the gap to managed platforms 'closes significantly with the right hosting and plugin discipline' — properly optimized WordPress can match Webflow's baseline. The ceiling is about the DEFAULT/unmanaged state, not an immovable hard cap.
counter.soWhat: Avoid implying the default-CMS tier is permanently slow. The honest claim is that the ceiling exists WITHOUT ongoing expert tuning — which is exactly the value a managed/purpose-built build provides. Lean on 'consistent performance without configuration,' not 'WordPress is slow.'

counter.point: GoHighLevel does ship genuinely useful scaling features for local lead-gen — local SEO heatmaps / geo-grid rank tracking, full funnel-to-conversion tracking in one workflow — and vendors concede it 'handles the full funnel' for most local/regional campaigns where the goal is conversion.
counter.soWhat: The GHL ceiling is real on PERFORMANCE, EXPORT/OWNERSHIP, and RENDERING — not on every axis. Scope the critique to those three; do not claim GHL is useless for local lead-gen, because for many operators it converts fine. Concede the funnel strength, win on the architectural ceiling.

allClaims.claim: WordPress's share of CMS-built sites DROPS as traffic scales — from 59.3% overall to 46.8% among the top-1,000 highest-traffic sites — evidence that the largest/most-trafficked web properties diversify OFF the dominant default-template CMS rather than staying on it.
allClaims.stat: WordPress: 59.3% overall vs 50.9% (top 10k) vs 46.8% (top 1k) of CMS-detected sites
allClaims.snippet: WordPress percentages by ranking: Overall 59.3%; Top 100,000 51.6%; Top 10,000 50.9%; Top 1,000 46.8%. WordPress's usage drops from 59.3% overall to 46.8% among the top 1,000 sites, suggesting larger sites opt for alternative solutions.

allClaims.claim: WordPress is the dominant default CMS overall — powering ~41.5% of all websites and ~59.3% of all sites with a known CMS — so the template/WordPress tier is genuinely the baseline most small contractors run on (the scaling argument is about the ceiling, NOT that templates can't exist or succeed).
allClaims.stat: ~41.5% of all websites; ~59.3% of CMS-detected sites (W3Techs, June 2026)
allClaims.snippet: WordPress is used by 59.3% of all the websites whose content management system we know. This is 41.5% of all websites.

allClaims.claim: Google's own spam policy explicitly targets 'doorway' pages and 'scaled content abuse' — multiple near-identical pages (e.g., city/location pages with little unique value) created mainly to rank. This is the exact failure mode of the templated lead-gen tier when it scales page count across markets.
allClaims.stat: Two named, enforceable spam categories: doorway abuse + scaled content abuse
allClaims.snippet: Doorway abuse: 'sites or pages are created to rank for specific, similar search queries... multiple domain names for specific regions that funnel users elsewhere.' Scaled content abuse: 'many pages are generated for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings and not helping users.'

allClaims.claim: Google's March 2026 spam update actively penalized auto-built location pages and near-identical city pages, while unique location-specific content was largely spared — confirming the template-sprawl ceiling is being enforced in practice, not just on paper.
allClaims.stat: March 24, 2026 spam update; targeted programmatic/auto-built location pages; recovery 3–6 months
allClaims.snippet: Google went after sites pushing out hundreds or thousands of AI-written pages with little or no editorial review, including programmatic SEO pages, auto-built location pages... Businesses using doorway pages saw major drops, including dozens of city pages with nearly identical copy, while legitimate local businesses with unique, location-specific content were mostly fine.

allClaims.claim: GoHighLevel — the canonical local-lead-gen template tier — offers NO supported website export. Sites are locked in its proprietary builder, so a contractor who scales and wants to migrate to a real CMS cannot cleanly take the site with them. This is a concrete, primary-sourced scaling/ownership ceiling.
allClaims.stat: Zero supported 1:1 export path (per GHL's own support portal)
allClaims.snippet: HighLevel does not support exporting websites in a way that allows them to be managed or edited outside the HighLevel platform... There is no supported 1:1 website export.

allClaims.claim: Demand for export off GHL is a documented, open pain point: contractors/agencies on GHL's OWN ideas board request the ability to move sites to WordPress/their own hosting if they leave — evidence the lock-in bites scaling businesses specifically.
allClaims.stat: Open, upvoted feature request on GHL's official ideas board
allClaims.snippet: Feature request: 'be able to export the website created in GHL outside GHL to clients current hosting service.' Users have stated they would build all their sites in GHL if they could have assurance of being able to export the site out to WordPress in the event a client wants to discontinue service.

allClaims.claim: GoHighLevel itself is positioned for agencies and small local service businesses (dentists, gyms, salons, local trades) — explicitly NOT enterprise. The vendor's own marketing concedes the tier: it is the consolidate-your-stack tool for sub-enterprise operators, which is exactly where a scaling multi-crew roofer outgrows it.
allClaims.stat: Self-positioned for agencies + small/local service businesses; HubSpot/enterprise framed as the larger-org alternative
allClaims.snippet: GoHighLevel was built specifically for agencies... If you're an agency owner, coach, course creator, or a local business like a dentist, gym, salon, or real estate agent, GoHighLevel is built with your needs in mind. (HubSpot positioned as the enterprise CRM for large teams with big budgets; GHL as the alternative for smaller organizations.)

allClaims.claim: Performance is a hard scaling ceiling with measurable lead impact: Google's own research found bounce probability rises sharply with load time (123% as load goes 1s→10s). Heavy multi-purpose template/builder stacks tend to be slower, and slowness directly costs mobile-heavy contractor traffic.
allClaims.stat: +123% bounce probability as load time goes 1s → 10s (Google/Think with Google)
allClaims.snippet: as page load time goes from one second to 10 seconds, the probability of a mobile site visitor bouncing increases 123%

allClaims.claim: The widely-cited '32% bounce increase from 1s→3s load' figure also traces to Google research, reinforcing the same direction at the load-times templates actually hit. (Use as directional support, not a precise promise — original 2017 Think-with-Google framing.)
allClaims.stat: +32% bounce probability, 1s → 3s load time
allClaims.snippet: the probability of bounce increases by 32% as page load time goes from 1 second to 3 seconds

allClaims.claim: Scaled contractors typically run a SPLIT stack: a marketing/website layer (WordPress, increasingly Webflow/headless for performance + custom UX) PLUS a separate operations layer (ServiceTitan/JobNimbus-class field-service CRM). The all-in-one template tier collapses both into one tool, which is the integration ceiling growing operators hit.
allClaims.stat: Two-layer pattern: marketing CMS + dedicated field-service ops platform
allClaims.snippet: ServiceTitan works best for established mid- to large-sized home service businesses that have office staff, multiple field technicians, and a reliable flow of jobs... it isn't a great option for sole proprietors or small businesses. Many businesses use WordPress for their website presence and ServiceTitan or similar tools for operations.

allClaims.claim: Webflow Enterprise is a documented home for scaled marketing sites needing performance + content scale: built on AWS + Fastly CDN, MACH-certified headless APIs, CMS Collections supporting hundreds of thousands of items — the kind of headroom a templated builder doesn't offer. (Capability is real; specific named roofing-brand stacks were NOT verified, so frame as platform capability/pattern, not a brand claim.)
allClaims.stat: Enterprise plans accommodate hundreds of thousands of CMS items; AWS + Fastly infra; headless APIs
allClaims.snippet: Webflow supports performant and scalable connections through MACH-certified, headless APIs... infrastructure is built on AWS for scalable computing power and uptime reliability, while Fastly handles global content delivery... enterprise plans accommodating hundreds of thousands of CMS items.

allClaims.claim: Independent SEO consensus: cookie-cutter templates create duplicate/near-duplicate content risk and Google's Sept-2025 spam wave hit identical-template city/region pages hardest — directly tying the content-ceiling argument to ranking outcomes, not aesthetics.
allClaims.stat: Identical-template multi-city sites flagged for lacking originality (Sept 2025 spam update)
allClaims.snippet: Websites that relied on repetitive, cookie-cutter content, especially across multiple pages, were hit hardest by Google's September 2025 Spam Update, with businesses using identical templates across different cities or regions flagged for lacking originality.

allClaims.claim: Independent, methodologically-rigorous data (HTTP Archive Web Almanac, Google-backed CrUX field data) shows WordPress — the dominant default template/CMS tier most small contractors run on — passes Google's Core Web Vitals on only ~40% of origins (2024), BELOW the 51% global average for all websites, while purpose-built managed platforms outperform it (Duda 73%, TYPO3 71%, Squarespace 60%, Wix 58%). The default template tier carries a measured performance ceiling relative to platforms engineered for scale.
allClaims.stat: WordPress good-CWV pass rate 40% (2024, up from 28% in 2023) vs 51% global average; Duda 73%, TYPO3 71%, Squarespace 60%
allClaims.snippet: WordPress had a 28% pass rate in 2023 and 40% in 2024 ... the global CWV pass rate for all origins as of June 2024 is 51% ... Duda (73%), TYPO3 CMS (71%), and Squarespace (60%) significantly outperform WordPress's 40% pass rate.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (CrUX field data, all origins on each CMS)

allClaims.claim: GoHighLevel — the canonical all-in-one local lead-gen template tier — has an architectural performance ceiling that no in-platform tuning can clear: typical GHL pages score 20–45 on mobile PageSpeed with Largest Contentful Paint of 4–8 seconds, and even after every available optimization the page 'will not score above 60 to 70' because users cannot enable server-side rendering or edge caching or reduce the shared JavaScript bundle — the platform controls those decisions. (Source sells GHL speed fixes, so vendor-incentive; the ceiling direction is independently corroborated by GHL's own support guidance, which only offers in-platform toggles and never claims SSR/edge control.)
allClaims.stat: GHL mobile PageSpeed 20–45 typical; LCP 4–8s; ~1,300ms main-thread JS block; max ~60–70 after optimization
allClaims.snippet: A typical GoHighLevel funnel page scores between 20 and 45 on mobile ... Typical LCP ranges from 4 to 8 seconds ... your GHL page will not score above 60 to 70 on Mobile PageSpeed. The architecture prevents it ... You cannot enable server-side rendering or edge caching. The platform controls those decisions.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (PageSpeed/Lighthouse) but vendor-reported, not independently audited

allClaims.claim: GoHighLevel's own support article on improving funnel/website page speed offers ONLY in-platform toggles a user can flip ('Optimise Javascript', 'Image optimisation', global CDN) and removing page fields/elements — it never offers control over rendering mode, server-side rendering, or edge caching. The vendor's own documentation thereby confirms the boundary of what a contractor can do: optimization stops at the toggles GHL exposes.
allClaims.stat: Speed levers offered = JS-optimize toggle, image-optimize toggle, CDN, fewer elements (no SSR/render control)
allClaims.snippet: Ensure 'Optimise Javascript' is enabled in funnel settings ... Ensure 'Image optimisation' is enabled ... HighLevel uses global CDN ... We optimized the data used to render pages by removing unnecessary fields from the page data response.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: directional (documents the boundary of user-controllable levers)

allClaims.claim: The roofing industry's own software vendor (ServiceTitan) and SEO consensus place WordPress and custom-built sites as the platforms 'serious roofing companies prioritizing lead generation and SEO scaling' choose — explicitly because open-source ownership, SEO control, custom design flexibility, and integration with contractor-specific field software are needed at scale. The template/builder tier is positioned as the fast-launch entry point, not the scaling endpoint — a roofing-specific framing of the headroom argument.
allClaims.stat: Industry framing: builders = fast launch ($100–300, <1 wk); WordPress/custom = scaling/SEO endpoint ($2,500–10,000+)
allClaims.snippet: For serious roofing companies prioritizing lead generation and SEO scaling, WordPress and custom-built solutions remain the top choices among industry leaders.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: directional (industry consensus, not a measured stat)

allClaims.claim: Webflow — a documented home for scaled, performance-sensitive marketing sites — passes Core Web Vitals at a materially higher rate (~58%, above the 51% global average) and averages ~2.3x faster LCP than WordPress, because managed hosting, a global CDN, and automatic image optimization deliver consistent performance with no per-site tuning. This is the measured performance gap between the default-CMS tier and a purpose-built scaling platform, not a claim about a specific brand's stack.
allClaims.stat: Webflow ~58% CWV pass (vs WordPress 36–40%); ~2.3x faster average LCP; documented WordPress→Webflow PageSpeed jumps 60–70 → 90–95
allClaims.snippet: Webflow sites pass Core Web Vitals approximately 58% of the time ... Webflow sites average 2.3x faster LCP scores due to cleaner code and optimized hosting compared to WordPress ... PageSpeed scores jump from 60–70 to 90–95 without additional work.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (CWV/LCP), but the 58% figure should be cross-checked against Web Almanac CMS data which independently shows the same direction

allClaims.claim: Client-side-rendered builder pages (the rendering model GHL and many template builders use) carry a 2026-specific scaling penalty beyond human SEO: most AI crawlers do not execute JavaScript, so a pure-CSR site can be effectively invisible to ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Claude — a new and growing discovery surface. SSR is now the zero-cost default in modern frameworks (Next.js, Astro, SvelteKit), so the CSR builder tier is falling behind on a dimension that did not exist a few years ago.
allClaims.stat: Most AI crawlers render no JavaScript; SSR vs CSR LCP gap on mid-range Android ~2–4s
allClaims.snippet: most AI crawlers don't render JavaScript at all — meaning a pure-CSR site can be invisible to ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Claude ... on mid-range Android devices the gap between SSR and CSR is often 2–4 seconds.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: directional / measured (LCP gap measured; AI-crawler-blindness is a documented behavior, magnitude varies by crawler)

pillars.title: Revenue / ROI math
pillars.section:
## P10 — Revenue / ROI Math

**Bottom line: one closed job pays for the system many times over. Everything past that is the client's own ticket times their own close rate times their own lead volume — a calculator they fill in, not a number we promise.**

### The per-lead value (modeled, revenue not profit)

Value-per-lead is a multiplication: ticket × close rate. Both inputs are public.

- A typical full roof replacement runs ~$9,500 nationally, typical range ~$5,900–$13,400 ([homeadvisor.com](https://www.homeadvisor.com/cost/roofing/install-a-roof/)). The Triangle skews higher — Raleigh standard asphalt commonly $8,000–$12,000, NC statewide average ~$10,900–$15,171 ([50northroofing.com](https://www.50northroofing.com/roof-replacement-cost-in-north-carolina-2026/)). A ~$20k ticket is defensible as a Triangle base case only for premium/metal/large or storm work, not for typical replacement.
- Organic/owned-channel roofing leads close at roughly 18–24% lead-to-job. Three unrelated lead-marketing vendors converge on that band ([pineconeleads.com](https://www.pineconeleads.com/blog/lead-generation-for-roofing-companies); [pipelineon.com](https://pipelineon.com/blog/construction-leads-guide/); [eliteseoconsulting.com](https://eliteseoconsulting.com/seo-vs-lead-aggregator-cost-comparison/)). Shared aggregator leads (Angi/HomeAdvisor) close at just 6–10% over the same sources — the "owned beats rented" gap.

Run the math honestly:
- Conservative: $9,500 × 15% ≈ **$1,425/lead**
- Realistic: $12,000 × 20% ≈ **$2,400/lead**
- Optimistic (storm/large/premium ticket): $18,000 × 25% ≈ **$4,500/lead**

The popular "$3–5k per lead" figure holds **only at the storm/premium ceiling** — it pairs the high-ticket end with the organic close rate. The realistic core is ~$2,400 ([homeadvisor.com](https://www.homeadvisor.com/cost/roofing/install-a-roof/)). And this is **revenue, not profit** — roofing net margins are thin, so $2,400 of revenue is not $2,400 of take-home.

### Cost of the system vs. the return

The software floor is small. GoHighLevel runs $97 / $297 / $497 per month = $1,164 / $3,564 / $5,964 per year ([gohighlevel.com](https://www.gohighlevel.com/pricing)). A single closed ~$10k job clears the $297/mo tier (~$3,564/yr) roughly 3× over. That is the real frame: tool cost is a rounding error against one job. It is **not** a claim that the $297 tool generates the revenue — the revenue requires the full build plus ongoing off-page ops (GBP, reviews, links).

### Timeline — this compounds, it does not start hot

SEO is a cold-start. Only 1.74% of newly published pages reach Google's top 10 within a year, 72.9% of top-10 pages are 3+ years old, and the average #1 page is 5 years old ([ahrefs.com](https://ahrefs.com/blog/how-long-does-it-take-to-rank-in-google-and-how-old-are-top-ranking-pages/)). Model it as ramp, not flat: months 0–3 near-zero, partial through months 4–9, approaching steady state around month 12, compounding after. Fast partial wins are possible on low-competition long-tail/location terms — 40.82% of pages that *do* reach top-10 get there within a month — but most pages never rank at all ([ahrefs.com](https://ahrefs.com/blog/how-long-does-it-take-to-rank-in-google-and-how-old-are-top-ranking-pages/)). The slow ramp is a feature for a defensible deck: it sets the expectation so the client doesn't ask why month 2 isn't paying yet.

### Annual revenue — a sensitivity table, not a headline

Annual revenue = value-per-lead × lead volume. Volume is the biggest swing variable and is **not controllable by the site alone** — it depends on market size, competition, and off-page ops. Present it as a table the prospect fills with their own realistic volume:
- 3 qualified organic leads/mo: ~$51k / $86k / $162k per year (conservative / realistic / optimistic)
- 6/mo: ~$103k / $173k / $324k per year

These leads-per-month figures are **illustrative placeholders**, flagged as such ([homeadvisor.com](https://www.homeadvisor.com/cost/roofing/install-a-roof/)).

### Does owned-channel SEO return positively for trades? Directionally, yes

One vendor's proprietary client data puts Construction SEO at ~681% ROI / 5-month break-even and HVAC at ~678% / 6-month — faster than their cross-industry median ([firstpagesage.com](https://firstpagesage.com/reports/seo-roi-statistics-fc/)). Use this as **directional** evidence that trades SEO breaks even fast and returns positively — never as a promised multiple. The ratio bakes in an assumed ~$120k/yr agency cost on the vendor's own un-third-party-verified portfolio, so it does not transfer to our offer. Tie any ROI claim to the client's **own** ticket × close × volume.

**What NOT to oversell:** Don't headline "$3–5k per lead" (that's the storm/premium ceiling, not the base — lead with ~$2,400). Never call value-per-lead "profit." Don't quote 681%/748% as what a client will get. Don't imply the $297 tool produces the revenue, or that any single annual number is a promise — close rate, ticket, and volume are all the client's variables, and the ramp is slow on purpose.

loadBearing.claim: Realistic value-per-lead for owned-channel roofing is ~$2,400 (revenue), modeled as a ~$12,000 ticket times a 20% organic close rate; the conservative-to-optimistic band runs ~$1,425 to ~$4,500. The popular '$3-5k per lead' figure holds only at the storm/large/premium ceiling.
loadBearing.stat: VPL: conservative ~$1,425 ($9.5k x 15%); realistic ~$2,400 ($12k x 20%); optimistic ~$4,500 ($18k x 25%) — REVENUE per qualified lead, not profit
loadBearing.snippet: On average, roof replacement costs $9,601 ... Most homeowners spend between $5,900 and $13,367 for a full roof replacement
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the central deck number — the per-lead value the entire ROI story rests on. It's also the single most-overstated input (storm-ticket x organic-close mismatch yields the misleading $3-5k). Getting the honest ~$2,400 core on the slide is what survives a skeptic and the FTC.
loadBearing.measured_or_modeled: modeled (ticket measured, close rate directional, product modeled)

loadBearing.claim: Organic/owned-channel roofing leads close at roughly 18-24% lead-to-job, with three unrelated lead-marketing vendors converging on that band; shared aggregator (Angi/HomeAdvisor) leads close at just 6-10%. This supports the 15-25% close band used in the model.
loadBearing.stat: Organic/SEO 18-24% close; shared aggregator (Angi/HomeAdvisor) 6-10% close
loadBearing.snippet: Shared leads from Angi and HomeAdvisor close at 6-10% ... organic search leads close at 18-24% ... Referral close rates run 35-50%+
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Close rate is the other multiplicand in value-per-lead and the basis for the 'owned beats rented' contrast. Three unrelated vendors converging on ~18-24% is the strongest defense of the band — but all carry a selling incentive, so it must be framed as client-controlled, never a King Maker promise.

loadBearing.claim: SEO revenue must be modeled cold-start to maturity, not flat from month one: only 1.74% of newly published pages reach Google's top 10 within a year, 72.9% of top-10 pages are 3+ years old, and the average #1 page is 5 years old.
loadBearing.stat: 1.74% of new pages rank top-10 within a year; 72.9% of top-10 pages 3+ yrs old; avg #1 page = 5 yrs old; 40.82% of eventual top-10 pages rank within 1 month
loadBearing.snippet: Only 1.74% of newly published pages rank in the top 10 within a year ... 72.9% of pages in Google's top 10 are more than 3 years old ... The average #1 ranking page is 5 years old
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: The only truly independent (non-vendor) anchor in the corpus, and the one that inoculates the whole deck: it justifies the cold-start ramp and pre-empts the 'why am I not making $86k in month 2' objection. Cuts AGAINST fast-revenue hype, which is exactly why a skeptic and the FTC find it credible.

loadBearing.claim: The software-layer cost is a rounding error against one job: GoHighLevel runs $97/$297/$497 per month ($1,164/$3,564/$5,964 per year), and a single closed ~$10k roof clears the most-popular $297/mo tier (~$3,564/yr) roughly 3x over.
loadBearing.stat: GHL annual: $1,164 / $3,564 / $5,964; one ~$10k job clears the $297 tier (~$3,564/yr) ~3x over
loadBearing.snippet: Starter $97 /Month ... Unlimited $297 /Month MOST POPULAR ... Agency Pro $497 /Month
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the 'cost objection killer' slide. It's a primary-source price against a measured ticket. Load-bearing precisely because it's apples-to-oranges (tool cost vs revenue outcome) and must be framed as 'tool cost is small vs one job,' never 'GHL generates the revenue' — the honest framing is what keeps it defensible.
loadBearing.measured_or_modeled: modeled (price primary, ticket measured, comparison framing)

loadBearing.claim: Owned-channel SEO returns positively and breaks even fast for the trades, directionally: one vendor's proprietary client data puts Construction SEO at ~681% ROI / 5-month break-even and HVAC at ~678% / 6-month — but the ratio bakes in an assumed ~$120k/yr agency cost on un-third-party-verified data and must not be quoted as a promised multiple.
loadBearing.stat: Construction ~7.40 ROAS / 681% ROI / 5-mo break-even; HVAC ~8.15 ROAS / 678% ROI / 6-mo; cross-industry median ~748%
loadBearing.snippet: Construction ROAS 7.40, ROI 681%, time-to-break-even 5 months ... Median SEO ROI 748% ($7.48 per $1)
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: The only industry-specific MEASURED SEO ROI anchor — tempting to headline. Load-bearing as a trap: it must be presented as directional ('trades SEO breaks even fast and returns positively') and never as the ratio a client will get, because the inputs don't transfer to King Maker's lower-cost offer and the data is the vendor's own unaudited portfolio.
loadBearing.measured_or_modeled: measured (single vendor's own client portfolio; not third-party verified)

whatNotToOversell: Don't headline '$3-5k per lead' as the base case — it only appears when you pair the storm/premium ticket with the organic close rate. Lead with the realistic ~$2,400 and show $4,500 only as the storm/premium ceiling.

Never call value-per-lead 'profit,' 'earnings,' or 'take-home.' It is REVENUE. Roofing net margins are thin (~5-15%), so $2,400 revenue is not $2,400 to the owner. Conflating the two is an FTC-grade overstatement.

Don't present annual revenue ($51k/$86k/$162k etc.) as a promise or a single headline number. Lead volume — the biggest driver — depends on market, competition, and off-page ops the site doesn't fully control. Present it as a sensitivity table the prospect fills in with their own volume; the 3/6-leads-per-month figures are illustrative placeholders.

Don't quote 681% / 748% / 5-month break-even as the ROI a client will get. It's one vendor's un-third-party-verified portfolio with an assumed ~$120k/yr cost baked in. Use it only as directional evidence that trades SEO returns positively, tied to the client's own ticket x close x volume.

Don't imply the $297/mo GHL tool generates the revenue. The delta proves tool cost is small vs one job — not that the tool equals the outcome. The modeled revenue requires the full build plus ongoing off-page ops.
Don't promise fast revenue. The Ahrefs ramp data (1.74% of new pages rank top-10 in a year) says cold-start is long. Use it to set expectations months 0-12, not to oversell speed.

Mark every close-rate and deal-size figure as vendor-incentive sourced; lean on the convergence of three unrelated vendors plus the independent Ahrefs study, and present close rate as a client-controlled variable, never a King Maker guarantee.
gaps: No truly independent (non-vendor) measured dataset for roofing lead-to-job close rate by channel. Best available is convergence across 3 marketing-agency sources; a contractor-survey or platform first-party dataset (e.g., a CRM provider's aggregate) would harden this.
No sourced distribution for organic lead VOLUME per month for a typical local roofer's site at maturity — the single largest input to annual revenue is modeled/assumed, not sourced.

No roofing-specific NET MARGIN source captured this pass, so the revenue->profit step is intentionally not modeled. A margin benchmark (e.g., contractor financial benchmarking) is needed before any 'profit' claim.

Charlotte/NC-specific ticket and CPL figures not isolated — all ticket/close data is national. Regional adjustment (NC labor/material costs, storm frequency) would tighten the model for the Peak Roofing demo.

The Ahrefs ranking study is general-web, not roofing/local-pack specific. Local-pack (GBP) ranking timelines can be faster than organic-page timelines; a Sterling Sky / Whitespark local-ranking-time source would better fit local contractor SEO.

The widely-cited '14.6% inbound close rate' traces to older HubSpot/marketing-stat lineage and was not run down to a primary measured study this pass; treated as directional only and not used as a load-bearing number.

No independent, third-party-verified (non-vendor) measurement of roofing/contractor SEO ROI was found — every ROI ratio traces to an SEO agency with a selling incentive (First Page Sage, searchscaleai, etc.). The pillar's ROI claims remain directional, not audited.
No NC/Triangle-specific organic close-rate or value-per-lead measurement exists; close-rate bands are national industry benchmarks applied to local ticket data (modeled, not measured locally).

No clean public data isolates the incremental revenue from a SITE specifically (vs the full GBP+reviews+links+ads stack). All ROI figures bundle on-page SEO with off-page work, so attributing revenue to King Maker's site deliverable alone is not directly supported.

The seed's $3-5k value-per-lead is only reachable at the premium/metal/storm Triangle end (~$20k ticket x 25% close); the realistic Triangle core lands ~$2.6k. Round 1's caveat stands — no new source moves the conservative/realistic core into the $3-5k band.

Lead VOLUME (qualified organic leads/month) remains the single biggest, least-sourced swing variable — it depends on market size, competition density, and off-page execution, none controllable by the site alone. No defensible per-market volume benchmark was found.

counter.point: Nearly all sourced close-rate and deal-size figures come from marketing agencies/lead vendors with a selling incentive (Pinecone, Inquirly, Elite SEO, Pipeline On). They have an interest in making organic/owned channels look strong vs aggregators.
counter.soWhat: Mark these source_type vendor-incentive and lean on the convergence of THREE unrelated vendors landing at ~18-24% organic close, plus the truly-independent Ahrefs ramp study. Present close rate as a client-controlled variable, never a King Maker promise.

counter.point: The seed's chain ('~$20k ticket x 15-25% close -> $3-5k value-per-lead') silently uses the storm/premium ticket with the organic close rate. Typical replacement is ~$9.5k-$13k, which yields a $1.4k-$2.6k value-per-lead — the $3-5k only appears at the large/premium/insurance end.
counter.soWhat: Do NOT headline $3-5k/lead as the base case. Lead with the realistic ~$2,400 and show $4,500 only as the storm/premium optimistic ceiling. Mismatching ticket-end with close-rate-end is exactly the move a skeptic/FTC would flag.

counter.point: Value-per-lead is REVENUE, not profit. Roofing net margins are thin (often ~5-15% after materials/labor/overhead), so $2,400 revenue/lead is NOT $2,400 of owner take-home.
counter.soWhat: Always label the model 'revenue,' never 'profit' or 'earnings.' If the deck implies margin, cite a margin source separately. Conflating the two is an FTC-grade overstatement.

counter.point: Lead VOLUME — the biggest driver of annual revenue — is essentially unsourced and uncontrollable by the website alone. It depends on market size, competition density, and off-page factors (GBP, reviews, links) that King Maker doesn't fully own.
counter.soWhat: Present annual revenue as a PER-LEAD-times-VOLUME sensitivity table the prospect fills in with their own realistic volume, not a single headline number. The 3/6 leads-per-month figures are illustrative placeholders, explicitly flagged.
